questions.q: The energy of a photon of frequency $f$ is:
questions.solution:
$E = \mathbf{hf} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, with $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}$ J s.

Energy comes in discrete packets, and the size of each packet depends on the frequency alone.

questions.q: Increasing the intensity of light of fixed frequency increases:
questions.solution:
Intensity is the **number of photons per second**, so it governs how many electrons are emitted — not how energetic each is.

The kinetic energy is fixed by the **frequency**: $E_{k,\max} = hf - \phi$.
options: the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons
the number of photoelectrons per second

questions.q: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of momentum $p$ is:
questions.solution:
$\lambda = \mathbf{\dfrac{h}{p}}$.

Everything has one, but for anything macroscopic it is around $10^{-34}$ m — far too small to produce any observable effect.

questions.q: An electron falling between two energy levels emits a photon of energy:
questions.solution:
$hf = E_{1} - E_{2}$, the **difference** between the levels.

Because the levels are discrete, only certain differences are possible — which is why atoms emit **line** spectra rather than a continuous range, and why each element's spectrum is a fingerprint.

questions.q: The activity of a radioactive sample is:
questions.solution:
$A = \mathbf{\lambda N}$ — the decay constant times the number of undecayed nuclei, in becquerels.

As $N$ falls, so does the activity, and both decay exponentially with the same half-life.

questions.q: Find the energy (in eV) of a photon of wavelength $400$ nm. Take $hc = 1240$ eV nm.
questions.solution: $E = \dfrac{1240}{400} = \mathbf{3.1}$ eV — violet light, at the edge of the visible range.

questions.q: Light of photon energy $4.5$ eV falls on a metal of work function $2.3$ eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, in eV.
A nuclide has a decay constant of $0.0231$ s$^{-1}$. Find its half-life, in s.
A sample contains $10^{12}$ undecayed nuclei with decay constant $10^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$. Find the activity, in $10^{9}$ Bq.
questions.solution: $A = \lambda N = 10^{-3} \times 10^{12} = 10^{9}$ Bq, so the answer is $\mathbf{1}$.

questions.q: Find the energy (in MeV) equivalent to a mass defect of $0.005$ u. Take $1$ u $= 931.5$ MeV/c$^{2}$.
Describe the photoelectric effect, state the observations that the wave theory cannot explain, and show how the photon model accounts for each.
questions.solution:
**The effect.** Electrons are emitted from a metal surface when light of a high enough frequency falls on it.

**Three observations wave theory cannot explain.**

1. **A threshold frequency exists.** Below it, no electrons are emitted however intense the light or however long you wait.

**Wave theory predicts** that any frequency should work eventually, as energy accumulates.

**Photon model:** one photon gives all its energy $hf$ to one electron. If $hf < \phi$, no single photon can free it, and energy from two photons is not pooled.

2. **Emission is instantaneous** — within about $10^{-9}$ s, even in very dim light.

**Wave theory predicts** a delay of minutes or hours while enough energy arrives.

**Photon model:** the transaction is a single event, so there is nothing to wait for.

3. **Maximum kinetic energy depends on frequency, not intensity.**

**Wave theory predicts** that brighter light carries more energy and should give faster electrons.

**Photon model:** brighter means **more photons**, not more energetic ones. Each electron still receives exactly $hf$.

**Einstein's equation:**

$hf = \phi + E_{k,\max}$

**The decisive test.** A graph of stopping potential against frequency is a straight line of gradient $\dfrac{h}{e}$ — the **same for every metal** — with its intercept on the frequency axis at the threshold.

Millikan set out to disprove Einstein's equation and ended by measuring $h$ with it.

questions.q: Explain wave-particle duality, and describe the evidence for the wave nature of electrons and the particle nature of light.
questions.solution:
**The idea.** Both radiation and matter show **wave** behaviour in some experiments and **particle** behaviour in others. Neither picture alone is complete; which one appears depends on what is being measured.

**Evidence for the wave nature of electrons — the Davisson-Germer experiment.** Electrons accelerated through a known potential were fired at a nickel crystal, and the scattered beam showed clear **diffraction maxima**.

Diffraction is a wave phenomenon that particles cannot produce. The wavelength deduced from the pattern agreed with $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}$ to within one per cent.

**Its practical consequence:** the electron microscope. Accelerated electrons have wavelengths thousands of times shorter than light, so they resolve detail an optical microscope never could.

**Evidence for the particle nature of light — the photoelectric effect.** The existence of a threshold frequency, the instantaneous emission, and the independence of electron energy from intensity all require light to arrive in discrete quanta.

**Also the Compton effect**, in which an X-ray photon colliding with an electron loses energy and changes wavelength exactly as a billiard-ball collision would predict.

**How to hold the two together.** The wave model describes how radiation **propagates** — interference, diffraction, refraction. The particle model describes how it **interacts** with matter — emission and absorption.

The two never contradict each other in a single experiment, because no experiment shows both at once. Light is neither a wave nor a particle in the everyday sense; those are two familiar models we borrow to describe something that is neither.

questions.q: State the law of radioactive decay, derive $N = N_{0}e^{-\lambda t}$, explain why decay is random yet predictable, and describe how the half-life is found from a graph.
questions.solution:
**The law.** The rate of decay is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present:

$-\dfrac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N$

**Derivation.** Separating and integrating from $N_{0}$ at $t = 0$:

$\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dN}{N} = -\lambda\int dt$

$\ln\dfrac{N}{N_{0}} = -\lambda t$

$\mathbf{N = N_{0}e^{-\lambda t}}$

**Half-life.** Putting $N = \dfrac{N_{0}}{2}$:

$t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}$

**Random yet predictable.** It is impossible to say **which** nucleus will decay next or **when** any particular one will. A nucleus does not age: its chance of decaying in the next second is the same as it was a thousand years ago.

Yet a sample contains perhaps $10^{20}$ nuclei, and with such numbers the **statistical** behaviour is precise. It is the same reason a life insurer can predict how many claims it will receive without knowing who will make them.

**The randomness is directly observable** as the irregular clicking of a Geiger counter, and as the fluctuation in repeated counts of the same sample.

**Finding the half-life from a graph.** Plot **$\ln A$ against $t$**, giving a straight line of gradient $-\lambda$. Then $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}$.

The log plot uses every point, averages out the counting fluctuations, and confirms that the decay really is exponential — which reading a single half-life off the curve would not.

**Do not forget to subtract the background count** before plotting; it is always present and it does not decay.

questions.q: Define mass defect and binding energy, explain the binding energy per nucleon curve, and show why both fission and fusion release energy.
questions.solution:
**Mass defect.** The mass of a nucleus is **less** than the total mass of its separate nucleons.

$\Delta m = Zm_{p} + Nm_{n} - M_{\text{nucleus}}$

**Binding energy** is the energy equivalent of that missing mass, $E = \Delta mc^{2}$ — the energy needed to pull the nucleus completely apart, or released when it is assembled.

**Binding energy per nucleon** is the meaningful comparison between nuclei, since it measures how tightly each nucleon is held.

**The curve.** It rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks at about $8.8$ MeV per nucleon near $A = 56$ (iron and nickel), then falls slowly to about $7.6$ MeV at $A = 238$.

A **higher** value means a **more stable** nucleus, so iron sits at the bottom of the energy valley.

**Fission.** A heavy nucleus at $7.6$ MeV per nucleon splits into two middling ones at about $8.5$ MeV per nucleon. Each of $236$ nucleons becomes more tightly bound by roughly $0.9$ MeV, releasing around $200$ MeV in total.

**Fusion.** Two very light nuclei, low on the steeply rising part of the curve, combine into one much higher up. The gain **per nucleon** is far larger than in fission — which is why the Sun outperforms any reactor.

**Both processes move matter towards $A = 56$**, from either direction. Energy is released whenever nucleons roll downhill into a deeper well.

**And nothing can be released beyond iron**, which is why fusion in a dying star stops there — and why everything heavier than iron was made in the supernova that followed.

questions.q: Explain how discrete energy levels give rise to line spectra, and distinguish emission from absorption spectra.
questions.solution:
**Discrete levels.** An electron in an atom can occupy only certain energy levels. It cannot sit between them — the intermediate energies simply do not exist for it.

**Emission.** When an electron falls from a higher level to a lower one, the difference is carried away as a single photon:

$hf = E_{2} - E_{1}$

Because only certain differences are possible, only certain frequencies appear — **bright lines** on a dark background.

**Absorption.** White light passed through a cool gas loses exactly those photons whose energy matches a level difference, since only they can lift an electron between levels.

The result is a continuous spectrum crossed by **dark lines**, at precisely the frequencies the same gas would emit.

**Why the lines coincide.** The same energy gaps govern both processes — one going up, the other coming down.

**Why this matters.** Every element has a unique set of levels and therefore a unique spectrum — a fingerprint that identifies it at any distance.

**Helium was discovered in the Sun** before it was found on Earth, from an unexplained line in the solar spectrum in 1868. Its name comes from **helios**.

The composition of stars, the expansion of the universe (through the redshift of known lines), and the presence of particular molecules in interstellar clouds are all read from spectra.

**And it was the line spectrum of hydrogen that forced quantum theory into existence:** classical physics predicted a continuous spectrum and an atom that collapsed in $10^{-8}$ s. Discrete energy levels were the answer to both.
